title: "Poisson mixed effects models"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}

We now combine three ideas developed earlier: [Poisson regression](poisson-regression.qmd) models a count, an [exposure offset](exposure-offsets.qmd) converts that count into a rate comparison, and a [random intercept](random-intercepts.qmd) represents the fact that the English and French sides of one aligned passage share material.

The count's [conditional probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd) distribution and [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) are defined after the aligned pair deviation is supplied. The [group deviation framework](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) treats that deviation as a draw from a population. The resulting likelihood keeps the observed graph counts fixed while comparing coefficient and variance values.

The basic idea is to compare Scene rates while pairing translations. A pair intercept lets the two sides of an unusually Scene dense passage move together rather than attributing their shared increase to language. The first aligned pair below makes the count, exposure, and rate calculation concrete with observed graph measurements.

Sulem, Abend, and Rappoport's [French-English UCCA study](https://aclanthology.org/W15-3502/) compares independently annotated passages from *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea*. The annotation follows [Universal Conceptual Cognitive Annotation](https://aclanthology.org/P13-1023/) (UCCA). A UCCA Scene contains a Process or State main relation; it is not simply a finite clause or verb token.

The analysis below uses the graph counts in the current table and answers a paired rate question; it does not attempt to reproduce the passage averages reported in the earlier study.

## Stating the observation and target

One row is one complete passage graph in English or French. `pair_id` joins the aligned translations. As defined in the [UCCA passage measures](../statistical-inference/paired-observations.qmd#ucca-passage-measures), `word_count` counts nonpunctuation Layer-0 word nodes, while `terminal_count` additionally counts punctuation terminals. `scene_count` counts distinct nodes with an outgoing Process or State edge. A remote reference to an existing node does not create another Scene. <!-- dqr-allow: reference-metadata -->

The table contains graph-aware counts but no passage text. We can therefore inspect the first aligned pair without inventing a sentence:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-ucca-pair
ucca_preview <- read.csv("data/ucca-french-english/passage-counts.csv")
ucca_preview$scene_rate <- with(
  ucca_preview,
  scene_count / word_count
)
ucca_preview[ucca_preview$pair_id == ucca_preview$pair_id[[1L]], c(
  "pair_id", "language", "release_passage_id", "word_count",
  "scene_count", "scene_rate", "scene_count_primary_main_relation", "remote_edge_count",
  "participant_primary_edge_count", "participant_remote_edge_count"
)]
```

To count Scenes in a graph, inspect every foundational node and mark it once if it has an outgoing Process (`P`) or State (`S`) edge. A node with both a primary mention and a remote reference is still one node and thus one Scene. Counting proceeds over nodes. Verbs, clauses, and `P` or `S` edge tokens do not supply the counting units.

The target is the French to English Scene rate ratio among these passages, conditional on variation across aligned passage pairs. The primary rate uses annotated words other than punctuation as exposure. A refit using all terminals checks the consequence of also counting punctuation in the exposure.

## Assembling the conditional model

The [population coefficient](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd#beginning-with-the-scientific-target)
below describes the systematic French-versus-English contrast. The random
intercept introduces a normal distribution for pair-specific deviations. For
fixed observed graph counts, the [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd#probability-and-likelihood)
is their joint model mass viewed as a function of those coefficients and variance
parameters; `glmer()` maximizes an approximation to the likelihood after
integrating over the unobserved pair deviations.

For passage pair $p$ and language side $l$,

$$
Y_{pl}\mid b_p
\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{pl}),
$$

with probability mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_{pl}=y\mid b_p)
=\frac{\exp(-\lambda_{pl})\lambda_{pl}^{y}}{y!}.
$$

The log expected count combines word exposure, a language contrast, and the pair intercept:

$$
\log\lambda_{pl}
=\log W_{pl}
+\beta_0
+\beta_1\operatorname{French}_{pl}
+b_p,
$$

where

$$
b_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2).
$$

The notation $Y_{pl}\mid b_p$ uses [conditional probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd): it treats the pair deviation as given when describing a row. The parameter $\tau_p^2$ is the [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#variance-as-expected-squared-distance) of the modeled pair-deviation distribution.

Exponentiating gives

$$
\lambda_{pl}
=W_{pl}
\exp\left(
\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{French}_{pl}+b_p
\right).
$$

Dividing by exposure shows the modeled Scene rate:

$$
\frac{\lambda_{pl}}{W_{pl}}
=\exp\left(
\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{French}_{pl}+b_p
\right).
$$

The offset fixes the coefficient of $\log W_{pl}$ at one. Doubling word exposure doubles the expected count while holding the rate constant.

## Fitting the paired UCCA model

The function `glmer()` fits a generalized linear mixed model. Here `family = poisson(link = "log")` supplies the conditional count distribution and log link, while `(1 | pair_id)` adds one intercept deviation for each aligned pair. The setting `nAGQ = 1` requests the [Laplace approximation](laplace-approximation.qmd), which approximates the integral over those pair deviations using the height and curvature near each conditional mode. Finally, `bobyqa` names the numerical search algorithm used for the outer optimization. These settings tell the software how to fit the stated probability model; they do not add linguistic assumptions.

```{r}
#| label: fit-ucca-poisson
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

ucca <- read.csv("data/ucca-french-english/passage-counts.csv")
ucca$pair_id <- factor(ucca$pair_id)
ucca$language <- factor(
  ucca$language,
  levels = c("en", "fr")
)

fit <- glmer(
  scene_count ~ language +
    offset(log(word_count)) +
    (1 | pair_id),
  data = ucca,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  nAGQ = 1L,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

terminal_fit <- glmer(
  scene_count ~ language +
    offset(log(terminal_count)) +
    (1 | pair_id),
  data = ucca,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  nAGQ = 1L,
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

data_summary <- c(
  graph_rows = nrow(ucca),
  aligned_pairs = nlevels(ucca$pair_id),
  english_scenes = sum(ucca$scene_count[ucca$language == "en"]),
  french_scenes = sum(ucca$scene_count[ucca$language == "fr"])
)
data_summary

language_coefficient <- lme4::fixef(fit)[["languagefr"]]
french_english_rate_ratio <- exp(language_coefficient)
terminal_rate_ratio <- exp(
  lme4::fixef(terminal_fit)[["languagefr"]]
)
c(
  french_log_rate_coefficient = language_coefficient,
  french_english_rate_ratio_per_word = french_english_rate_ratio,
  sensitivity_rate_ratio_per_terminal = terminal_rate_ratio
)
```

The mathematical pieces map to the fitting call as follows:

| Model term | R formula term | Role |
|---|---|---|
| $Y_{pl}$ | `scene_count` | observed Scene count |
| $\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{French}_{pl}$ | `language` | population log-rate contrast |
| $\log W_{pl}$ | `offset(log(word_count))` | fixed one-for-one exposure adjustment |
| $b_p$ | `(1 \| pair_id)` | aligned-pair deviation |
| Poisson with log link | `family = poisson(link = "log")` | conditional count distribution and mean map |

The fitted rate comparison comes from the coefficients above; the numerical settings only determine how the software searches for those estimates.

Holding the passage-pair effect fixed, the fitted French Scene rate is `r sprintf("%.3f", french_english_rate_ratio)` times the fitted English rate per annotated word. The comparison is multiplicative because the model uses a log link.

With all Layer-0 terminals as exposure, the corresponding ratio is
`r sprintf("%.3f", terminal_rate_ratio)`. The two fits use
the same Scene counts and pair structure. Their difference comes only from whether
punctuation contributes to the opportunity denominator.

## Showing observed counts and fitted rates

The points below are observed passage counts. The fitted curves set the pair deviation to zero and vary word exposure, so the observations and model remain on the same count scale.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ucca-poisson
prediction_grid <- expand.grid(
  word_count = seq(
    min(ucca$word_count),
    max(ucca$word_count),
    length.out = 180L
  ),
  language = factor(
    c("en", "fr"),
    levels = levels(ucca$language)
  )
)
prediction_grid$population_fitted_scenes <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = prediction_grid,
  type = "response",
  re.form = NA
)

ggplot(
  ucca,
  aes(x = word_count, y = scene_count, shape = language)
) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4, color = "grey35") +
  geom_line(
    data = prediction_grid,
    aes(
      y = population_fitted_scenes,
      linetype = language
    ),
    color = "#1F5A85",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Annotated words in passage",
    y = "UCCA Scenes",
    shape = "Language",
    linetype = "Language"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Preserving the conditioning statement

Conditional on $b_p$, the Poisson model has

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_{pl}\mid b_p]
=\mathbb{E}[Y_{pl}\mid b_p]
=\lambda_{pl}.
$$

This statement concerns a passage pair with a given deviation. A prediction for a new pair must average over the fitted pair distribution. We next show why that averaging produces [marginal overdispersion](overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd), even though the conditional response remains Poisson.

Every pair comes from consecutive material in one novel, one translation, and one
annotation history. The passages therefore share author, translator, genre, and
annotation context. The fitted rate ratio summarizes Scene counts in these aligned
graphs; the design supplies no independent sample of authors, translators, genres,
or language pairs from which to estimate a general French to English contrast.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why does a remote edge not create another Scene?
2. What comparison is made by the language coefficient after the offset is included?
3. Does `nAGQ=1` mean that the data contain one quadrature point?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. A remote edge refers to an already existing node. Scene counting marks distinct nodes with an outgoing Process or State edge. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. It compares French and English Scene rates per annotated word while holding the aligned-pair deviation fixed. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. No. It selects a Laplace approximation for integrating model random effects; it is a fitting setting. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>

We next separate conditional Poisson variation from [marginal dispersion](overdispersion-and-random-effects.qmd) induced by group variation.
